artiest/john-adams.text:
John Adams is an American composer and conductor, born in Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1947. He grew up in a musical family and came into contact with classical music, jazz, musicals and rock. As a child he played the clarinet and at ten he began to compose. He studied at Harvard, with Leon Kirchner, Roger Sessions and David Del Tredici among others, and took his bachelor's degree there in 1969 and his master's in 1971.

His earliest work was modernist, but he came to rebel against that. His style grows out of the minimal music of Steve Reich and Philip Glass, but he turns more readily to the big orchestral sounds and climaxes of late Romanticism, such as Wagner and Mahler. His works include Shaker Loops, Harmonielehre, Short Ride in a Fast Machine and Grand Pianola Music. His first opera, Nixon in China, tells of Richard Nixon's visit to China in 1972. It was the first of many works with director Peter Sellars. The reception was mixed at first, but the work enjoys ever greater respect and is performed worldwide. The Death of Klinghoffer followed, among others.

Adams is one of the most frequently performed living composers of contemporary classical music. Many of his operas deal with historical events. His importance for popular culture lies in the way he linked the repeating patterns of minimal music, which also fascinated pop musicians, with the full sound of a Romantic orchestra.
artiest/john-adams.listen: Listen to Short Ride in a Fast Machine and notice the continuous, ticking rhythm in the woodwinds and the gradually rising brass.

artiest/john-barbirolli.text:
Sir John Barbirolli was a British conductor and cellist, born Giovanni Battista Barbirolli in London in 1899, the son of an Italian father and a French mother. He grew up in a family of professional musicians and felt himself a Cockney all his life. He began on the violin at four, but soon switched to the cello, because as a child he walked around during practice. From 1912 to 1916 he studied at the Royal Academy of Music.

As a cellist he was given the chance to conduct from 1926, first with the British National Opera Company and then with the touring company of Covent Garden. He is best known as conductor of the Hallé Orchestra in Manchester. In 1943 he helped save the orchestra from disbandment and remained associated with it for the rest of his life.

Both in the concert hall and on record he was associated above all with the music of English composers such as Elgar, Delius and Vaughan Williams. His performances of late Romantics such as Mahler and Sibelius are also still admired, as is his Schubert. He recorded extensively, including Finlandia, the Karelia Suite and Valse triste by Sibelius, the Enigma Variations by Elgar and La Mer by Debussy. Barbirolli died in 1970. He stood for British orchestral culture, in which a local orchestra with a permanent conductor could shape a city.
artiest/john-barbirolli.listen: Listen to Elgar's Enigma Variations under Barbirolli and notice how each variation has its own character, like a short portrait sketch of a friend.

artiest/john-barry.text: John Barry, from York, led the pop group The John Barry Seven in the late 1950s. For Dr. No (1962) he arranged the James Bond theme by Monty Norman, with its famous twang guitar. He went on to write the music for eleven Bond films. With Goldfinger (1964) he fixed the Bond sound: sharp brass, jazz chords and a big title song. In The Ipcress File (1965) he used a cimbalom. Later his style became broader and more romantic, with long string melodies. Barry won five Oscars: two for Born Free (1966), and others for The Lion in Winter (1968), Out of Africa (1985) and Dances with Wolves (1990).
artiest/john-barry.listen: Notice the brass chords and jazz harmony in the Bond music, and the slow, broad string melodies in his later work.

artiest/john-bonham.text:
John Bonham was an English musician, the drummer of Led Zeppelin. He was known for his speed, power, fast single-foot bass drum and sense of groove, and is regarded as one of the greatest and most influential drummers of all time. He was born in Redditch, Worcestershire, in 1948. At five he built a drum kit out of tins and coffee cans, at ten he was given a snare drum and at fifteen a complete drum kit. He was largely self-taught and was influenced by Max Roach, Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich.

After school he worked as an apprentice carpenter for his father and played in local bands, including two with Robert Plant. In 1968, after the Yardbirds broke up, Jimmy Page formed a new band and Plant suggested Bonham. Page and manager Peter Grant saw him drumming for Tim Rose in a London club. Thus Led Zeppelin came into being, at first as the New Yardbirds.

You can hear his heavy playing on songs such as Immigrant Song, When the Levee Breaks, Kashmir and The Ocean, and in his drum solo Moby Dick, which often lasted twenty minutes. Later he added congas, timpani and a gong. Besides hard rock he also played funk and Latin influences. He also worked on records by Lulu, among others. Bonham died in 1980. He influenced drummers such as Dave Grohl, Neil Peart and Chad Smith.
artiest/john-bonham.listen: Listen to When the Levee Breaks by Led Zeppelin and notice the heavy, slow drum beat, which has an echo all its own and carries the whole song.

artiest/john-cage.text: John Cage, from Los Angeles, studied with Schoenberg and then worked in New York, often together with the choreographer Merce Cunningham. He placed screws and rubber erasers between the piano strings and so created the prepared piano, a percussion ensemble under ten fingers. Later he let the Chinese oracle book I Ching determine his compositions. His 4'33'' from 1952, in which the musicians stay silent, turns the sounds in the hall into the music.
artiest/john-cage.listen: Listen to the sonata and hear how the prepared piano sounds like a small gamelan orchestra of gongs, wood blocks and muffled bells.

artiest/john-cale.text:
John Cale is a Welsh musician, composer and producer, born in the mining village of Garnant in 1942. At home he spoke Welsh; he learned English only at primary school. He played organ in church and discovered a talent for the viola, with which he joined the National Youth Orchestra of Wales at thirteen. He studied music in London, became involved in the avant-garde movement Fluxus and left for New York in 1963.

There Cale took part in an eighteen-hour performance of Erik Satie's Vexations, together with John Cage. He also played in composer La Monte Young's Theatre of Eternal Music, which produced long, sustained tones: drones. With Lou Reed he then founded The Velvet Underground. On The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967) and White Light/White Heat (1968) he plays viola, bass and keyboards. Tensions with Reed led to his departure in 1968. He then produced the debut by The Stooges and albums by Nico, and made solo records such as Paris 1919 (1973), which is regarded as his masterpiece, and Fear (1974). In 1990 he made Songs for Drella with Reed, a tribute to Andy Warhol.

Cale brought the avant-garde into rock music. His amplified viola and his love of drones and dissonance gave The Velvet Underground a raw, experimental side that the band largely lost after his departure. As a producer he later worked with Patti Smith, The Modern Lovers and Happy Mondays, and so his influence remained felt in punk and alternative rock.
artiest/john-cale.listen: Listen to Venus in Furs (1967) by The Velvet Underground. Notice Cale's electric viola, which lays a scraping, sustained tone beneath the song.

artiest/john-carpenter.text: John Carpenter is a director, but also writes the music for his own films. He did so at first because there was no money for a composer. He plays synthesizers and piano and works with simple, constantly repeated motifs. For Assault on Precinct 13 (1976) he made a tight electronic rhythm. The theme of Halloween (1978) is a piano motif in an unusual 5/4 time, which keeps returning and builds the tension. From Escape from New York (1981) he worked with sound engineer Alan Howarth. Carpenter names Bernard Herrmann as a model. His minimal synthesizer sound influenced much later horror and synthwave.
artiest/john-carpenter.listen: Notice the short piano motif in five-beat time and the low synthesizer tones that repeat endlessly.

artiest/john-carpenter-en-alan-howarth.text:
John Carpenter is an American film director who often provides his films with music himself, mostly with synthesizers. Alan Howarth is an American composer and sound designer from Cleveland, Ohio. Howarth played in local rock bands and opened for groups such as The Who and Cream. From 1976 he provided synthesizer support to the fusion band Weather Report, which took him to Los Angeles. In 1980 came his breakthrough when his music was used for a trailer for a Star Trek film. He then worked on the next five Star Trek films.

Carpenter and Howarth worked together on Escape from New York (1981), Halloween II, Halloween III: Season of the Witch, Christine, Big Trouble in Little China, Prince of Darkness and They Live, among others. The Main Title of Escape from New York from 1981 belongs to that work. Howarth also did sound design for Star Trek: The Motion Picture, Raiders of the Lost Ark, Poltergeist and Total Recall, among others. His team won two Academy Awards for sound effects, for The Hunt for Red October and Bram Stoker's Dracula. He also performs his film music live to film clips.

The music of this duo is typical of the 1980s: a cold, repeating synthesizer pattern, a sober melody and a menacing bass, made with few resources. The style proved highly influential and returned in later electronic pop music, synthwave and film music. It shows how few notes are enough to build tension.
artiest/john-carpenter-en-alan-howarth.listen: Listen to the Main Title of Escape from New York and notice the repetition: how do a few synthesizer lines and a low bass together build a menacing atmosphere?

artiest/john-coltrane.text: John Coltrane grew up in North Carolina and Philadelphia. He named Lester Young, Charlie Parker and Dexter Gordon as important models. From 1955 he played in Miles Davis's quintet, in 1957 for a few months with Thelonious Monk, and then again with Miles on Kind of Blue. On Giant Steps (1959) he played over rapidly changing chords with a stream of notes that came to be called sheets of sound. In 1960 he started a quartet with pianist McCoy Tyner and drummer Elvin Jones; at the end of 1961 bassist Jimmy Garrison joined. He played My Favorite Things on the soprano saxophone and made a spiritual statement with A Love Supreme (1964). In his last years he played free jazz. He died in 1967.
artiest/john-coltrane.listen: On Giant Steps, try to hear the changes of key: fast and constantly different.

artiest/john-cougar-mellencamp.text:
John Mellencamp was born in Seymour, Indiana, in 1951. He formed his first band, Crepe Soul, when he was fourteen. After years in local bands he travelled back and forth between Indiana and New York until he met manager Tony DeFries of MainMan. DeFries released his debut Chestnut Street Incident in 1976 under the name Johnny Cougar, because Mellencamp would supposedly be too hard to sell. The album flopped. A short time in London followed, then A Biography in 1978 and the album John Cougar in 1979, on which I Need a Lover became his first American hit.

The breakthrough came in 1982 with American Fool. It includes Hurts So Good, which won a Grammy for best male rock vocal, and Jack & Diane, which spent four weeks at number one. In 1983 came Uh-Huh, on which he added his surname back for the first time. Later he dropped Cougar altogether. In the 1980s more hits followed, such as Crumblin' Down, Pink Houses, Small Town and R.O.C.K. in the U.S.A.

His music is called heartland rock: straightforward rock with traditional instruments and songs about small-town life in the American Midwest. In 1985 he was one of the founders of Farm Aid, the benefit concert for farmers who were in danger of losing their land. It still exists. In 2008 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted him. In 2018 the Songwriters Hall of Fame followed. He holds the record for the most number one hits by a solo artist on the Mainstream Rock chart.
artiest/john-cougar-mellencamp.listen: Listen to Jack & Diane and notice the guitar work and the hand claps in the chorus. Can you hear how a story about two teenagers in a small town carries the song?

artiest/john-deacon.text:
John Deacon is an English bassist, born in Leicester in 1951 and raised in Oadby. As a boy he already tinkered with electronics and loved soul music. At fourteen he played in the school band The Opposition, first on guitar and then on bass. In 1969 he went to London to study electrical engineering. In early 1971 he heard that a band had lost its bassist. After an audition in a lecture hall he became the last and youngest member of Queen, alongside Freddie Mercury, Brian May and Roger Taylor.

Deacon was chosen for his musicality, his calm character and his technical knowledge. He built the Deacy Amp himself, a small amplifier with which May created his layered guitar parts. From Sheer Heart Attack (1974) he wrote one or two songs on almost every album. You're My Best Friend, written for his fiancée, was on A Night at the Opera (1975). In 1980 he wrote Another One Bites the Dust, a dance song born of his love of soul, which was played on both Black and white radio stations. Later he also wrote I Want to Break Free and co-wrote Under Pressure.

Deacon was a quiet force in Queen. He brought soul and funk into the band and, together with Mercury, pushed Queen towards disco in the early 1980s. His bass lines are often simple, but so catchy that they carry a song. After Mercury's death in 1991 he performed a few more times, but in 1997 he stopped making music altogether.
artiest/john-deacon.listen: Listen to Another One Bites the Dust (1980) by Queen. Notice Deacon's bass line, which opens the song and keeps repeating, and how the rest of the band plays sparingly around it.

artiest/john-denver.text:
John Denver was born Henry John Deutschendorf Jr. in Roswell, New Mexico, in 1943. His father was an air force pilot, so the family moved often. At eleven he was given an acoustic guitar by his grandmother. His stage name came from Randy Sparks, founder of the New Christy Minstrels, who thought Deutschendorf did not fit on a billboard. Denver abandoned his architecture studies, moved to Los Angeles in 1963 and sang in folk clubs. In 1965 he succeeded Chad Mitchell in the Chad Mitchell Trio.

As a solo artist he made his debut in 1966 with John Denver Sings. Albums followed such as Rhymes & Reasons in 1969, Poems, Prayers & Promises in 1971 and Rocky Mountain High in 1972. His best-known songs are Take Me Home, Country Roads, Annie's Song, Rocky Mountain High, Calypso, Thank God I'm a Country Boy and Sunshine on My Shoulders. He wrote hundreds, about two hundred of them himself. He also appeared in television programmes and, in 1977, in the film Oh, God! alongside George Burns.

Denver sang mostly with acoustic guitar about nature, love and his dislike of city life. His music reached the country charts as well as the Hot 100 and the adult contemporary chart. He campaigned for the environment and for space exploration, and spoke before the United States Congress against censorship in music. Colorado made Rocky Mountain High a state song and West Virginia did the same with Take Me Home, Country Roads. He was killed in 1997 in a plane crash, in an aircraft he was piloting himself.
artiest/john-denver.listen: Listen to Take Me Home, Country Roads and notice how the acoustic guitar and the singalong chorus together evoke a warm, rural feeling.

artiest/john-eliot-gardiner.text:
Sir John Eliot Gardiner is an English conductor, born in Fontmell Magna, Dorset, in 1943. He grew up with singing in the family and in a church choir, played the violin and began conducting at fifteen. As a history student at Cambridge he conducted Monteverdi's Vespro della Beata Vergine in the chapel of King's College in 1964. Around that performance the Monteverdi Choir came into being. Later he studied in London and in Paris with Nadia Boulanger.

Gardiner built up three ensembles of his own. In 1968 he founded the Monteverdi Orchestra, which in 1977 switched to period instruments and in 1978 took the name English Baroque Soloists. In 1990 the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique followed, for nineteenth-century music. He was also music director of the Opéra National de Lyon and principal conductor of the North German Radio Orchestra. He recorded more than two hundred and fifty albums, mainly for Deutsche Grammophon, Philips and his own label Soli Deo Gloria.

His name is above all linked with Johann Sebastian Bach. In the year 2000, during the Bach Cantata Pilgrimage, he performed all of Bach's church cantatas, spread over a year and over churches in Europe and New York, in the order of the church year. He also wrote the book Music in the Castle of Heaven and presented the documentary Bach: A Passionate Life. In this way he helped bring period-instrument performance practice to a wide audience.
artiest/john-eliot-gardiner.listen: Listen to his 1982 recording of Handel's Water Music and notice the difference in tone colour between the Baroque wind instruments and a modern symphony orchestra.

artiest/john-entwistle.text:
John Entwistle was an English bassist, singer and songwriter, born in Hammersmith, London, in 1944. His father played trumpet and his mother piano. He had piano lessons, switched to trumpet at school and played horn in a youth orchestra. With his school friend Pete Townshend he played in a small jazz band. Because he could not hear his trumpet in a rock band, he chose the bass guitar, partly because of Duane Eddy's low guitar sound. He built his first bass himself.

Roger Daltrey asked Entwistle to be the bassist in his band The Detours, and Entwistle made sure that Townshend joined too. With drummer Keith Moon the group became The Who. On stage Townshend and Moon jumped around and smashed their instruments, while Entwistle stood still. To hear himself above the din, he was one of the first to use large stacks of Marshall amplifiers. He wrote a few songs on almost every Who album, such as Boris the Spider, and played horn and trumpet on records such as Tommy. In 1971 he was the first member of the band with a solo album, Smash Your Head Against the Wall.

Entwistle was the only member of The Who with a musical education. His nicknames were The Ox and Thunderfingers. He played the bass not as background, but as a lead instrument, with fast melodic lines and a sharp, high sound at full volume. In this way he became a model for generations of rock bassists. He died in 2002.
artiest/john-entwistle.listen: Listen to My Generation (1965) by The Who. Notice Entwistle's short bass solos between the vocals: here the bass plays the lead role instead of the guitar.

artiest/john-fogerty.text:
John Fogerty was born in Berkeley, California, in 1945 and grew up in El Cerrito. At high school in 1959 he formed a cover band, the Blue Velvets, with bassist Stu Cook and drummer Doug Clifford. Later his brother Tom joined. They took Little Richard, Bo Diddley and Carl Perkins as their models. In 1964 they signed to Fantasy Records, which, without their knowledge, changed the name to The Golliwogs. The seven singles they recorded under that name went unnoticed.

In 1968 the group became Creedence Clearwater Revival, with John as singer, lead guitarist and main songwriter. Susie Q was the first hit. Between 1968 and 1972 the band had nine singles in the top 10, including Proud Mary, Bad Moon Rising, Fortunate Son, Green River, Down on the Corner and Have You Ever Seen the Rain. In 1993 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted the group. When Creedence broke up in 1972, Fogerty began a solo career. Among the best known from it are The Blue Ridge Rangers from 1973 and Centerfield from 1985.

His style is called swamp rock: a raw voice, a flat, tight guitar sound and lyrics about rivers, the South and the ordinary American, even though he himself came from California. Many of his songs have been covered by artists from all kinds of genres. Rolling Stone placed him at number 40 among the greatest songwriters, and in 2005 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.
artiest/john-fogerty.listen: Listen to Bad Moon Rising and notice the contrast between the cheerful, fast guitar accompaniment and the ominous lyrics about disasters to come.

artiest/john-gilmore.text:
John Gilmore (1931 to 1995) was an American jazz saxophonist, clarinettist and percussionist. He grew up in Chicago and played clarinet from the age of fourteen. He took up the tenor saxophone during his service in the air force, from 1948 to 1951. In 1952 he toured with the Harlem Globetrotters, in an ensemble with pianist Earl Hines. A year later he met pianist and bandleader Sun Ra, and that determined the rest of his career.

For four decades Gilmore played and recorded almost exclusively with Sun Ra, first in a trio and then in the Sun Ra Arkestra. In the 1950s he led a band with Clifford Jordan, and in 1957 they recorded Blowing in from Chicago for Blue Note, with Horace Silver and Art Blakey among others in the rhythm section. He was also a sideman with Miles Davis, Art Blakey, Paul Bley, Andrew Hill and McCoy Tyner, among others. From 1964 to 1966 he played with Blakey's Jazz Messengers. After Sun Ra's death in 1993 he led the Arkestra until his own death.

Gilmore played both flexible, clear post-bop and abstract passages with shrill high squeals. John Coltrane, five years older, was impressed and took informal lessons from him in the late 1950s. Chasin' the Trane was inspired in part by Gilmore's sound. That he devoted his life to Sun Ra surprised some, because he could have become a big star. He saw Sun Ra's harmony as a logical continuation of bebop.
artiest/john-gilmore.listen: Listen to Blowing in from Chicago and notice Gilmore's broad, powerful tenor sound and the way he plays against the tight hard bop rhythm section.

artiest/john-hollingsworth.text:
John Hollingsworth (1916 to 1963) was a British conductor who worked in the concert hall, in ballet and opera and in the film studio. He was born in Enfield near London and studied at the Guildhall School of Music. In 1937, at the age of twenty-one, he conducted the London Symphony Orchestra, as its youngest conductor up to that time. During the war he served in the Royal Air Force, where he led the RAF Symphony Orchestra. With that orchestra he played six concerts at the Potsdam Conference.

After the war he worked at Rank under Muir Mathieson, on Brief Encounter and on William Walton's music for Hamlet, among others. From 1950 he conducted the Sadler's Wells Ballet. For ten years he was Sir Malcolm Sargent's right-hand man at the Proms, with 63 appearances and several world premieres. At Hammer Films he conducted horror films of the 1950s, such as Horror of Dracula and The Curse of Frankenstein, often with music by James Bernard. In 1955 he gave Richard Rodney Bennett the chance to write his first film score.

Hollingsworth made many recordings, mainly of ballet music and light orchestral music, including Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker with the Sinfonia of London. His place in music history is that of the craftsman in the background: he made sure that other people's scores sounded good, on stage, in the studio and on record.
artiest/john-hollingsworth.listen: Listen to his Nutcracker suite by Tchaikovsky and notice how clearly the conductor lets you hear the dance rhythms and the colours of the different orchestral sections.

artiest/john-lennon.text:
John Lennon was born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940 and grew up largely with his aunt Mimi. His mother Julia played Elvis Presley records for him and taught him to play the banjo. As a teenager he fell under the spell of skiffle, and in 1956 he founded The Quarrymen, the group that grew into The Beatles in 1960. Lennon sang the lead parts there together with Paul McCartney, played rhythm guitar and was at the beginning the effective leader. Their songwriting duo became the most successful in history.

From All You Need Is Love in 1967, his songs were sung by the counterculture and the movement against the war in Vietnam. In 1969 he started the Plastic Ono Band with his second wife, the artist Yoko Ono. That same year they held their bed-in for peace and Lennon left The Beatles. His first solo album John Lennon/Plastic Ono Band appeared in 1970, followed a year later by Imagine. Singles such as Give Peace a Chance, Instant Karma! and Happy Xmas (War Is Over) made him, as a solo artist too, a voice of the peace movement. In 1971 he moved to New York, where the Nixon administration spent three years trying to have him deported.

After five years of rest he returned in 1980 with Double Fantasy, which he made together with Ono. Three weeks after its release, on 8 December 1980, he was shot dead in New York. The album won the Grammy for album of the year a year later. As a writer or co-writer, Lennon had 25 number 1s on the American Billboard Hot 100.
artiest/john-lennon.listen: Listen to Imagine (1971). Notice how simply the song is built: a calm piano part carries the whole song, and Lennon sings his message of peace almost without emphasis.

artiest/john-lewis.text: The pianist and composer John Lewis played in Dizzy Gillespie's big band in the late 1940s and co-wrote Birth of the Cool. In 1952 he founded the Modern Jazz Quartet with vibraphonist Milt Jackson, bassist Percy Heath and drummer Kenny Clarke; Connie Kay succeeded Clarke in 1955. Lewis gave the group a form of its own: the musicians performed in suits, like a chamber ensemble, and played fugues and pieces in Baroque form alongside blues and bebop. He wrote Django in 1954 in memory of Django Reinhardt. Lewis was one of the most important figures of the third stream and also wrote film music, for instance for Odds Against Tomorrow.
artiest/john-lewis.listen: Hear how piano and vibraphone play two independent lines, as in Baroque music.

artiest/john-lowe.text:
John Charles Lowe, known to his friends as Duff, was an English pianist. He was born in 1942 and lived until 2024. He had known Paul McCartney since 1953. In February 1958 McCartney asked him to play piano with The Quarrymen, the Liverpool group that later grew into The Beatles. Lowe stayed with the band for two years.

His name is linked above all with one recording. In the studio that Percy Phillips had at home in Liverpool, the group recorded a disc for their own use, with two songs: That'll Be the Day and In Spite of All the Danger. Lowe kept the recording himself. In 1981 he sold it to Paul McCartney. McCartney had it remastered, and the two songs appear on The Beatles' album Anthology 1. It is thus one of the earliest surviving traces of the group.

In 1994 Lowe played with the Quarrymen once more, on the album Open for Engagements. Of that line-up, only he and guitarist Rod Davis had actually played in the group in the 1950s. Together with Davis, Len Garry and Colin Hanton he performed at Beatles events all over the world until 2017, under the name John Lennon's Original Quarrymen. His significance lies not in a career of his own, but in the preservation of a piece of Beatles history.
artiest/john-lowe.listen: Listen to That'll Be the Day on Anthology 1 and notice the rough recording quality: you hear a young group making a first record in a living-room studio.

artiest/john-lunn.text: John Lunn was born in Scotland in 1956. At the University of Glasgow he delved into twelve-tone technique, and at MIT he took computer music courses. In the 1980s he played bass and keyboards in Man Jumping, a group that mixed jazz, pop and world music. He also wrote operas, such as Misper (1997) and Zoë (2000) for Glyndebourne. For television he wrote music for Dickens serials such as Bleak House (2005) and Little Dorrit (2008). He became known for Downton Abbey (2010–2015). For that series he won an Emmy in 2012 and 2013. Later came Grantchester (2014) and The Last Kingdom (2015), among others.
artiest/john-lunn.listen: In Downton Abbey, listen to how piano and strings keep a steady, forward-moving rhythm, like a household that never stops running, beneath a broad melody.

artiest/john-mayall.text:
John Mayall was an English blues and rock musician, writer and producer. He was born in Macclesfield in 1933 and grew up in Cheadle Hulme. His father played guitar in local pubs. Mayall taught himself to play piano, guitar and harmonica, inspired by American blues musicians such as Lead Belly, Albert Ammons and Pinetop Smith. During his national service in Korea he bought his first electric guitar in Japan. Back in England he studied at the art school in Manchester and worked as a designer. Meanwhile he played with local musicians, including in the Powerhouse Four and the Blues Syndicate.

At the urging of Alexis Korner he became a professional musician in 1963 and moved to London. There he formed John Mayall & the Bluesbreakers, who played at the Marquee Club, with John McVie on bass among others. Over the years some of the most famous blues and blues-rock musicians of all would play in the group. His design experience came in handy for the sleeves of his albums.

Mayall was often called the godfather of British blues. His career spanned almost seven decades and he remained active until his death in 2024, at the age of ninety. In that year he was also inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. His importance lies above all in his work as a talent scout and bandleader: his Bluesbreakers became a training ground from which many British rock guitarists emerged, and he helped give American blues a British audience.
artiest/john-mayall.listen: Listen to Hideaway and notice the guitar: how does the instrumental melody run through the blues, and how does the band leave room for the soloist?

artiest/john-mclaughlin.text: The guitarist John McLaughlin grew up in England and as a boy fell under the spell of Django Reinhardt; later John Coltrane and Miles Davis were his great models. After years in London groups he recorded Extrapolation in 1969 and left for New York, where he played with Tony Williams's Lifetime and on Miles Davis's In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew. In 1971 he founded the Mahavishnu Orchestra, with lightning-fast unisons, odd time signatures and loud rock sounds. In the 1970s he led Shakti, an acoustic group with Indian musicians. He has a spiritual interest in India that colours all of his music.
artiest/john-mclaughlin.listen: Hear the fast, long lines of the guitar in interplay with violin or tabla.

artiest/john-paul-jones.text:
John Paul Jones, born John Baldwin, is an English bassist, keyboardist, arranger and producer, born in Sidcup in 1946. His father was a pianist and arranger for big bands and taught him to play piano from the age of six. At fourteen he was a church organist and choirmaster, and he bought his first bass guitar. He listened to the blues of Big Bill Broonzy, the jazz of Charles Mingus and the piano music of Rachmaninoff.

In 1962 he began playing with Jet Harris and Tony Meehan, and from 1964 he worked as a session musician at Decca. Until 1968 he played and arranged on hundreds of recordings, sometimes three a day. He worked for Donovan on Sunshine Superman, for Dusty Springfield, Cat Stevens and Herman's Hermits, and wrote the string arrangement for She's a Rainbow by The Rolling Stones. He got his stage name from Andrew Loog Oldham. In 1968 he asked Jimmy Page, whom he knew from the sessions, whether he could use a bassist. With Robert Plant and John Bonham they formed Led Zeppelin, in which Jones played bass, organ and piano.

Jones was the quiet craftsman of Led Zeppelin. His musical training and his experience as an arranger gave the band's heavy blues rock more colour, with keyboards, strings and unusual instruments. After the band ended in 1980 he worked as a producer and arranger and made solo albums such as Zooma (1999). Later he played in Them Crooked Vultures, with Dave Grohl and Josh Homme.
artiest/john-paul-jones.listen: Listen to Black Dog (1971) by Led Zeppelin. Notice the twisting riff that guitar and bass play together and that seems to change rhythm again and again.

artiest/john-philip-sousa.text:
John Philip Sousa was born in Washington, D.C., in 1854, the third of ten children. His father played trombone in the Marine Band and enrolled him in the band as an apprentice at thirteen, so that he would not join a circus orchestra. Sousa learned violin, piano, flute, brass instruments and voice, and turned out to have perfect pitch. After his service he worked as a violinist and learned to conduct in a theatre orchestra.

In 1880 he returned as leader of the Marine Band and stayed for twelve years. He made it the best military band in the country, with more symphonic repertoire and stricter rehearsals, and conducted under five presidents. In 1892 he founded the civilian Sousa Band. During the First World War he led the Naval Reserve Band in Illinois. His best-known marches are The Stars and Stripes Forever, Semper Fidelis, The Liberty Bell, The Thunderer and The Washington Post. He also helped develop the sousaphone, a marching tuba.

Sousa is called The March King. His marches sound clear and sturdy: a driving rhythm, plenty of brass and a melody that sticks. The Stars and Stripes Forever is the national march of the United States, Semper Fidelis that of the Marine Corps. From 1880 until his death in 1932 he did nothing but conduct and compose. His work laid the foundation for the wind band in American musical culture.
artiest/john-philip-sousa.listen: Listen to The Stars and Stripes Forever and notice the high little flute, the piccolo, which in the final themes sounds out above the rest of the brass.

artiest/john-philip-sousa-marine-band-of.text:
John Philip Sousa was an American composer and conductor, best known for his military marches. He wrote 136 marches, from 1873 until his death in 1932. A British journalist called him The March King, after the example of Johann Strauss II, the Waltz King. He wrote marches for various American universities and led the Marine Band from 1880 to 1892, with which he played at the inauguration celebrations of presidents James Garfield and Benjamin Harrison. He then founded a civilian band of his own and toured for the next 39 years.

His best-known work is The Stars and Stripes Forever from 1896. In 1987 it became, by an Act of Congress, the national march of the United States. The performance in the collection is by the Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy, a Dutch wind band, which shows that this American march is also played in Europe.

A Sousa march has a fixed form: a clear metre, a short introductory theme, repeated sections and a final section in which a high flute rises above the brass. The light, fast flute part in The Stars and Stripes Forever, the piccolo, is famous. Sousa made wind music into a popular genre, and his marches formed the basis of the wind band tradition in America and far beyond. They also influenced early jazz, because the first jazz bands in New Orleans began with marching instruments and march rhythm.
artiest/john-philip-sousa-marine-band-of.listen: Listen to The Stars and Stripes Forever and notice the piccolo in the final section: how does it fly above the heavy brass and the drums?

artiest/john-phillips.text:
John Phillips, also called Papa John, was born on Parris Island in South Carolina in 1935 and grew up in Alexandria, Virginia. At school he sang doo-wop with friends. He went to naval academy, but left in his first year, and later also dropped out of Hampden-Sydney College. In the early 1960s he moved to New York. There he played in The Journeymen, a folk trio with Scott McKenzie and Dick Weissman. They made three albums. In Greenwich Village he met Denny Doherty and Cass Elliot, the later members of his next group.

That was The Mamas & the Papas. Phillips wrote most of the songs and devised the arrangements, with two-part harmonies that move in opposite directions. At Dunhill the group had six top 10 hits, including California Dreamin', Monday, Monday, Creeque Alley and Dedicated to the One I Love. They split up in 1968. Phillips also wrote San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair) for his old friend Scott McKenzie in 1967 and Me and My Uncle, a staple of the Grateful Dead. As a solo artist he released John, the Wolf King of L.A. in 1970.

His best-known deed outside the songs is the Monterey International Pop Music Festival of June 1967. He helped organise it and performed there himself. It was meant to give rock music the same status as jazz and folk and is regarded as the first big pop festival ever. Together with Lou Adler he made the film Monterey Pop.
artiest/john-phillips.listen: Listen to California Dreamin' and notice how the four voices complement one another, and which melody line the men sing and which the women.

artiest/john-powell.text: John Powell was born in London in 1963 and studied violin at Trinity College of Music. He first wrote music for advertising and was an assistant to Patrick Doyle. In 1997 he moved to Los Angeles, where Face/Off became his first major film. With Harry Gregson-Williams he wrote Antz (1998) and Chicken Run (2000). For The Bourne Identity (2002) he first made a score without orchestra, with percussion, guitars and electronics. Later a string section was added. He continued that action style in the following Bourne films. He also wrote a great deal of music for animated films, such as Kung Fu Panda with Hans Zimmer and How to Train Your Dragon (2010), for which he received an Oscar nomination.
artiest/john-powell.listen: Notice the contrast between the driving rhythms of percussion, guitar and electronics in the Bourne films and the broad orchestral melodies in the animated films.

artiest/john-robie.text:
John Robie is an American keyboardist, producer and songwriter. His career began in the early 1980s in New York, when hip hop and club music there were seeking new forms. Robie was the man behind the synthesizers and had an experimental view of electronic music.

In 1982 he co-wrote Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force, which he made together with producer Arthur Baker. Robie provided the synthesizers and was called a wizard on that instrument in the press. The song borrowed melodies and rhythms from the German group Kraftwerk and put a hard electronic beat beneath them. He then produced Looking for the Perfect Beat and Renegades of Funk for the same group; the latter was later covered by Rage Against the Machine. With songs such as One More Shot by C-Bank and Body Mechanic by Quadrant 6, which he wrote and produced, he helped shape a new genre: electro. Later he worked for artists such as Chaka Khan, New Order, UB40 and Boy George.

The New York Times wrote in 1984 that Robie and Baker had reinvented the dance record, with sharp synthesizer sounds, rattling electronic percussion and electronically distorted voices. Producer Rick Rubin called Planet Rock one of the most influential songs ever. Robie's electro became a building block for hip hop, house and techno, and his songs were later sampled by Snoop Dogg, LL Cool J and Calvin Harris, among others.
artiest/john-robie.listen: Listen to Planet Rock (1982) by Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force. Notice the cool synthesizer melody and the hard, dry hits of the drum machine, and how the raps lie over them.

artiest/john-stepan-zamecnik.text:
John Stepan Zamecnik was born in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1872, the son of Czech immigrants. In the mid-1890s he studied at the Prague Conservatory with Antonín Dvořák and completed his training in 1897. In 1899 he returned to the United States. In Cleveland he worked as a violinist and composer, and he played violin in the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra under Victor Herbert. He wrote much of his work under pseudonyms, including Dorothy Lee, Lionel Baxter and Hal Vinton.

In 1907 he became music director of the new Hippodrome Theater in Cleveland. When silent films were shown there, he began writing music for them. Publisher Samuel Fox released it in the series Sam Fox Moving Picture Music. It consisted of separate pieces and motifs for pianists, organists and orchestras, such as Mysterious Burglar Music for the moment when a burglar comes into view. Fox was the first publisher in the United States to publish original film music. Zamecnik also wrote music for films such as The Covered Wagon and Wings and for wind bands, such as the march World Events from 1935.

His march World Events was given a second life when Jack Shaindlin, music director of Movietone News, used the first theme for the signature tune of the Movietone newsreels. Jackie Gleason used that version in the 1950s for a sketch. In 2011 Paramount received the original manuscript of Wings from the Library of Congress, after which a new recording was released in 2012 with the DVD and Blu-ray. Zamecnik died in 1953.
artiest/john-stepan-zamecnik.listen: Listen to the 2012 album Wings and notice how the music has to translate dramatic moments on screen, such as aerial combat and suspense, into sound without a word being spoken.

artiest/john-stevens.text:
John Stevens (1940 to 1994) was an English drummer and co-founder of the Spontaneous Music Ensemble. He was born in Brentford, the son of a tap dancer. As a child he listened to jazz, but drawing and painting attracted him more. At nineteen he joined the Royal Air Force, where he had drum lessons at the music school in Uxbridge. There he met Trevor Watts and Paul Rutherford, two people with whom he later collaborated a great deal.

In the mid-1960s he played in London jazz groups, including with Tubby Hayes and Ronnie Scott. When he heard the American free jazz of Ornette Coleman and Albert Ayler, he left traditional jazz behind. In 1966, with Watts and Rutherford, he founded the Spontaneous Music Ensemble, which played in a theatre club in central London. The first album, Challenge, appeared in 1967. He then became interested in the music of Anton Webern and the group began to play more quietly. Non-Western music also attracted him. He played on Life with the Lions by John Lennon and Yoko Ono, together with John Tchicai.

Stevens devised starting points for improvisation that were not compositions. The Click Piece asked each player to play the shortest possible note, over and over. From 1983 he took his way of making music to youth clubs and psychiatric institutions, with Community Music. The book Search and Reflect, made for the Open University in 1985, is an account of that. He died in 1994 of a heart attack.
artiest/john-stevens.listen: Listen to a recording by the Spontaneous Music Ensemble, such as John Stevens Spontaneous Music Ensemble from 1969, and notice the silences and the short, soft sounds with which the players respond to one another.

artiest/john-taylor.text:
John Taylor is an English bassist, born in 1960 in the Birmingham area. In 1978, in that city, he founded the band Duran Duran with keyboardist Nick Rhodes, named after a character in the science-fiction film Barbarella. Taylor began on guitar, but switched to bass guitar. Later singer Simon Le Bon, guitarist Andy Taylor and drummer Roger Taylor joined. Despite the shared surname, the three Taylors are not related.

Duran Duran broke through in 1981 with Planet Earth and became one of the biggest bands of the 1980s, with songs such as Girls on Film, Hungry Like the Wolf, Rio and The Reflex. The band belonged to the New Romantics, a movement with striking clothing and make-up, and put a great deal of work into music videos, which were shown on MTV. In 1985 Taylor also played in the side project The Power Station, with singer Robert Palmer. Later he left Duran Duran for a time, but he returned in the 2000s.

As a bassist Taylor drew inspiration from funk and disco. His bass lines are mobile and danceable, and give Duran Duran's synth-pop a solid groove. In this way he shows how the new wave of the 1980s borrowed from the Black dance music of the 1970s.
artiest/john-taylor.listen: Listen to Planet Earth (1981) by Duran Duran. Notice Taylor's funky, constantly moving bass line and the guitar with chorus effect, and how together with the synthesizers they form the beat.

artiest/john-tchicai.text:
John Tchicai (1936 to 2012) was a Danish free jazz saxophonist and composer. He was born in Copenhagen, the son of a Danish mother and a Congolese father, and grew up in Aarhus. He learned the violin and from his mid-teens played clarinet and alto saxophone, with a preference for the latter. In the late 1950s he travelled through northern Europe. In 1962 he met trumpeter Bill Dixon and saxophonist Archie Shepp at a festival in Helsinki. On their advice he moved to New York a year later.

There he took part in the October Revolution in Jazz and in the New York Contemporary Five and the New York Art Quartet. He can be heard on influential recordings such as Four for Trane by Shepp, New York Eye and Ear Control by Albert Ayler and Ascension by John Coltrane. In 1966 he returned to Denmark and focused on music education. He founded the orchestra Cadentia Nova Danica, in 1968 co-founded the Instant Composers Pool in Amsterdam and in 1969 played on Life with the Lions by John Lennon and Yoko Ono.

In the early 1980s he chose the tenor saxophone as his main instrument. In 1990 he received a lifelong grant from the Danish Ministry of Culture. He later lived in California and in the south of France and played in Yo Miles, a group that explored Miles Davis's electric period. Tchicai shows how free jazz from America also found a path of its own in Europe, with Denmark and the Netherlands as its home base.
artiest/john-tchicai.listen: Listen to Cadentia Nova Danica from 1970 and notice how many musicians play at once without the whole falling apart.

artiest/john-tilbury.text:
John Tilbury is a British pianist, born in 1936. He went to school in west London and studied piano at the Royal College of Music, and then with Zbigniew Drzewiecki in Warsaw. In 1968 he won the Gaudeamus competition in the Netherlands. In the 1960s he worked closely with the composer Cornelius Cardew and played in the Scratch Orchestra. His biography of Cardew, Cornelius Cardew: A Life Unfinished, appeared in 2008.

Since 1980 Tilbury has been a member of AMM, a group for free improvisation. He is regarded as one of the most important interpreters of the music of Morton Feldman. He also recorded work by Howard Skempton and John White and performed adaptations of Samuel Beckett's radio plays. On The Hands of Caravaggio, an album with the ensemble M.I.M.E.O. led by his AMM colleague Keith Rowe, he plays piano while another member simultaneously plays and mutes the strings. Duos for Doris from 2003, a collaboration with Rowe, is regarded as a milestone in electro-acoustic improvisation.

Tilbury fits both in the world of contemporary classical music and in that of improvisation. His playing is soft, concentrated and leaves much room for silence. In 2018, at the age of eighty-two, he stopped performing. He lives in Deal, Kent. He was then recorded at home for several more years, and part of those recordings was released in May 2026 as a four-disc box set.
artiest/john-tilbury.listen: Listen to Duos for Doris and notice the interplay between piano and electronics, and how long sounds are allowed to die away before something new comes.

artiest/john-williams.text: John Williams (born in 1932) studied at Juilliard and first worked as a jazz and studio pianist in Hollywood. With Jaws (1975) he showed how much tension two alternating notes in the double basses can generate. For Star Wars (1977) he reached back to the big symphony orchestra of the 1930s and 1940s, with leitmotifs for characters as in Wagner and Korngold. That did not fit the fashion for pop soundtracks, but it became an enormous success. Superman (1978) by Richard Donner followed, among others, as well as Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) and E.T. (1982), the last two with Steven Spielberg. For Schindler's List (1993) he chose a restrained violin solo. He won five Oscars.
artiest/john-williams.listen: Listen to the leitmotifs: short, recognisable themes that belong to a character, played by a full symphony orchestra with plenty of brass.

artiest/johnny-carisi.text:
John Carisi (1922 to 1992) was an American trumpeter and composer. He grew up in Jamaica, a neighbourhood in Queens, New York, and taught himself trumpet while playing in dance bands. He worked in Herbie Fields's orchestra and in Glenn Miller's Army Air Force Band. After the war he played with Ray McKinley, Claude Thornhill, Charlie Barnet, Urbie Green and Benny Goodman, among others. He also took lessons from the composer Stefan Wolpe.

His best-known piece is Israel, a minor blues that Miles Davis recorded during the sessions that later became known as Birth of the Cool. Bill Evans and Gerry Mulligan's Concert Jazz Band also recorded it. A second well-known piece is Springsville, which Miles Davis played in Gil Evans's arrangements on the album Miles Ahead. In 1957 Carisi wrote the arrangements for All About Urbie Green. He shared an album with Cecil Taylor, which appeared in 1961 on Impulse! as Into the Hot under Gil Evans's name, and in 1960 his own album The New Jazz Sound of Show Boat appeared. In 1968 he arranged Machinations by Marvin Stamm.

Carisi was not a bandleader with many recordings, but a composer whose few pieces went on resonating for a long time. Israel is regarded as a unique piece of jazz from the movement known as Cool Jazz. He also taught, first at Queens College and then at the Manhattan School of Music. He died in 1992 after heart surgery.
artiest/johnny-carisi.listen: Listen to Israel in the version by Miles Davis from the Birth of the Cool sessions and notice how dark and tight a blues can sound in a small orchestra with tuba and horn.

artiest/johnny-cash.text:
Johnny Cash was an American singer and songwriter, born in Kingsland, Arkansas, in 1932, into a poor family of cotton farmers. From the age of five he worked in the fields, where the family sang as they worked. His childhood revolved around gospel and the radio. His mother and a friend taught him to play guitar, and at twelve he wrote his first songs. As a serviceman in the air force in West Germany he formed his first band.

In 1954 Cash moved to Memphis. With guitarist Luther Perkins and bassist Marshall Grant he went to Sam Phillips's Sun Records. There he wanted to record gospel, but Phillips saw more in his rockabilly. In 1955 Hey, Porter and Cry! Cry! Cry! were released, followed by Folsom Prison Blues and I Walk the Line. In 1958 he moved to Columbia. Later came Ring of Fire, duets with his wife June Carter, such as Jackson, and concerts in prisons, such as at Folsom. At the end of his life he recorded songs by rock artists, including Hurt by Nine Inch Nails.

Cash had a deep, calm bass-baritone and a backing band with a driving, chugging guitar rhythm, like a train. His songs were about sorrow, guilt and redemption, and he took the side of the poor and of prisoners. Because he always performed in black, he was called the Man in Black. His music joined country, rock 'n' roll, blues, folk and gospel. He died in 2003.
artiest/johnny-cash.listen: Listen to I Walk the Line (1956). Notice the simple, rolling rhythm of guitar and bass and Cash's low, calm voice, which changes key with each verse.

artiest/johnny-clarke.text:
Johnny Clarke is a Jamaican reggae singer, born in 1955. He grew up in Whitfield Town, a poor district of Kingston. In 1971 he won a talent contest in Bull Bay. The prize was a meeting with producer Clancy Eccles, with whom a year later he recorded his first song, God Made the Sea and the Sun. It sold badly. With Rupie Edwards he had his first hits in 1973, Everyday Wondering and Julie. In 1974 he began a long collaboration with producer Bunny Lee and his band The Aggrovators. None Shall Escape the Judgement was an immediate success and gave his debut album its title.

In 1975 and 1976 he was named Artist of the Year in Jamaica. He mixed his own songs with covers of other reggae songs and combined roots with love songs. Many of his lyrics are about his faith as a Rastafarian, such as Let Go Violence, against violence, and Legalize It, about legalising marijuana. In 1976 he was one of the first Jamaican artists at Frontline, Virgin's label, where Authorized Version and Rockers Time Now appeared. In 1983 he moved to London and worked there with Mad Professor, among others.

Clarke helped shape the so-called Flying Cymbals period, which preceded the Roots Rockers sound of the mid and late 1970s. On stage he hides his knee-length dreadlocks, his African Roots, under a large hat and takes it off at the end of the concert. In 2012 he released an album on his own label Hit Machine for fifty years of Jamaican independence. He continues to perform.
artiest/johnny-clarke.listen: Listen to None Shall Escape the Judgement and notice the high, pleading voice above the rhythm section of bass and drums, which keeps repeating the same pattern.

artiest/johnny-clarke-king-tubby-en-the-.text:
This trio stands for Jamaican reggae of the mid-1970s. Johnny Clarke is a Jamaican singer, The Aggrovators were producer Bunny Lee's studio band, and King Tubby was the sound engineer who reworked the recordings. Little is recorded about Clarke and the band in the source available, so the text focuses mainly on King Tubby.

King Tubby, born Osbourne Ruddock in 1941, was a radio repairman in Kingston, with a workshop on Drumalie Avenue. He built large amplifiers for the sound systems, Jamaica's mobile discos, and constantly modified their equipment. He used separate amplification for bass and treble and built special equipment for echo and reverb. In 1968 he started his own sound system, Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi, which became popular for the quality of its equipment, exclusive records and his own echo and reverb. The career of the toaster U-Roy also began there. In 1968 he also became a disc cutter for producer Duke Reid.

Tubby reworked existing recordings into instrumental mixes. He brought vocals and instruments forward or made them disappear, and added echo and reverb. This is how dub came into being. He is often named as the inventor of the concept of the remix, which later became commonplace in dance and electronic music. The singer Mikey Dread said that Tubby understood sound in a scientific sense. Tubby died in 1989. A Ruffer Dub from 1975 is an example of his work: a track in which the mixer is almost an instrument.
artiest/johnny-clarke-king-tubby-en-the-.listen: Listen to A Ruffer Dub and notice what disappears and comes back: how do the bass and the drums surface, and where do you hear echo and reverb on individual sounds?

artiest/johnny-dodds.text: The clarinettist Johnny Dodds played in New Orleans with Kid Ory and then left for Chicago, where he joined King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. His brother Baby Dodds played drums in the same band. Johnny Dodds played with a full, warm tone in the low register and a strong feeling for the blues. He played clarinet on Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings and in 1926 and 1927 made records with groups of his own, such as the New Orleans Wanderers and the Black Bottom Stompers. He stayed in Chicago for his whole career, where he also ran a taxi business, and died there in 1940.
artiest/johnny-dodds.listen: Listen to the clarinet that circles around the melody and makes the blues sing.
